title: Abstract Algebra
text:
Preface
This book is a personal working reference on abstract algebra. Its purpose is to collect definitions, examples, proofs, interpretations, applications, and pedagogical observations in a form that can be revised continually.
The organization follows mathematical dependencies rather than a fixed teaching schedule. Some chapters may remain incomplete while others develop into detailed expositions. ## Why Abstract Algebra?
Abstract algebra begins with a simple observation: mathematical objects that appear very different may nevertheless behave in the same way. Integers can be added, symmetries can be composed, matrices can be multiplied, and permutations can be performed successively. The objects and operations differ, but many of the resulting patterns are identical.
The purpose of abstraction is to identify these shared patterns. We deliberately set aside features that are irrelevant to a particular question and retain only the properties that govern the operations under study. A group, for example, does not specify whether its elements are numbers, matrices, permutations, or geometric transformations. It records the structural rules that their operation satisfies. Any theorem proved from those rules then applies simultaneously to every example satisfying them.
This is the central economy of abstract algebra: one argument can replace many apparently unrelated arguments. More importantly, abstraction reveals relationships that are difficult to see when each example is considered in isolation. It allows us to ask:

When do two mathematical systems have the same structure?
Which properties are preserved when one system is mapped into another?
How can a complicated object be understood through its substructures or quotients?
Which features distinguish objects that otherwise appear similar?
What conclusions follow from the structural axioms alone?

These questions lead to the principal ideas of the subject. Isomorphisms express structural sameness. Homomorphisms compare algebraic systems while preserving their operations. Subgroups and subrings identify smaller structures contained within larger ones. Quotient structures systematically treat certain elements as equivalent. Group actions translate symmetry into algebra, while invariants help determine what can and cannot change under a given transformation.
Abstract algebra therefore does more than provide a language for calculation. It offers methods for classification, comparison, and proof. It can explain why certain constructions are possible, why others are impossible, and why the same phenomenon recurs in number theory, geometry, linear algebra, combinatorics, and the study of equations. Its applications to cryptography, coding theory, and computation are important, but they are consequences of the structural theory rather than its sole justification.
The subject is best approached through a continual movement between examples and abstraction. Concrete examples suggest definitions; definitions isolate the essential structure; general theorems are then tested and interpreted through further examples. The aim is not to move away from familiar mathematics, but to understand what its examples have in common and how far their shared structure can take us.

1.0.1 Order and the well-ordering principle
The integers are among the most familiar objects in mathematics. We learn to calculate with them long before we ask why their arithmetic has the form that it does. Familiarity, however, can conceal structure. In this chapter, we step back from calculation and examine the principles on which arithmetic in () rests.
Our purpose is not to review elementary arithmetic. Instead, we will ask questions such as:
The starting point is the well-ordering principle: every nonempty set of positive integers has a least element. This apparently simple property has powerful consequences. It gives a method for proving existence, underlies mathematical induction, and leads to a proof of the Division Algorithm. The Division Algorithm, in turn, produces the Euclidean algorithm, Bézout’s identity, and much of the elementary theory of divisibility.
Congruence modulo (n) introduces a further change of perspective. Rather than studying integers individually, we group together integers that have the same remainder upon division by (n). The resulting congruence classes form the set (/n), where addition and multiplication can be performed directly on classes. This will provide our first substantial example of a quotient construction.
Thus, the integers serve two purposes. They supply concrete examples against which later definitions can be tested, and they illustrate the process of abstraction itself: familiar operations and patterns are isolated, expressed as general principles, and then transported to new mathematical settings.
